name: Makes And The Product
description: After returning from the army Makes received a gift — an array a consisting of n positive integer numbers. He hadn't been solving problems for a long time, so he became interested to answer a particular question: how many triples of indices ( i , j , k ) ( i < j < k ), such that a i · a j · a k is minimum possible, are there in the array? Help him with it!
input_specification: The first line of input contains a positive integer number n (3 ≤ n ≤ 10 5 ) — the number of elements in array a . The second line contains n positive integer numbers a i (1 ≤ a i ≤ 10 9 ) — the elements of a given array.
output_specification: Print one number — the quantity of triples ( i , j , k ) such that i , j and k are pairwise distinct and a i · a j · a k is minimum possible.
approach_summary: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to N using Fermat's Little Theorem (mod 10^9+7 or 998244353). Answer nCr queries in O(1) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 817B — Makes And The Product [310. Large Factorials and Binomial Coefficients]
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Combinatorial selection $\binom{N}{K} = \frac{N!}{K!(N-K)!} \pmod P$ can be evaluated in $O(1)$ by precomputing factorials $fact[i] = fact[i-1] \cdot i \pmod P$ and inverse factorials $invFact[i] = invFact[i+1] \cdot (i+1) \pmod P$ using Fermat's Little Theorem $a^{P-2} \equiv a^{-1} \pmod P$.
